speechtext: AYLESWORTH moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 159) to amend the Exchequer Court Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not able to state with exactness the provisions of this Bill as I have not seen a copy of it, but I understand that the shape in which it finally passed the Senate was an extension of the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court to include the case of accidents which may happen not merely upon the line of government railways, but, speaking generally, in consequence of the operation of such railways. That is the scope of the enactment as it is now presented to this House.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Hon. FRANK OLIVER moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 163) to amend the Volunteer Bounty Act, 1908.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purpose of the Bill is to extend the time during which the scrip issued under the Volunteer Bounty Act may be located from the end of the year 1910 to the end of the year 1911. There are two minor amendments which do not affect the principle of the Bill, and which can be explained fully in committee.

Does this extension apply to scrip that is already sold and in the

hands of speculators, or does it apply only to scrip in the hands of volunteers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no distinction in the original Act between scrip that is in the hands of volunteers and scrip that is in the hands of speculators, and neither is there any distinction in the amendment to the Act.

I might point out to the minister what he very well knows1 that owing to the very short time that was given a great many of these volunteers to locate their land they found it absolutely impossible to do so. This war was brought to a close in 1902. Year after year this matter was brought to the attention of the government, and year after year we were met with the statement that the government had not decided whether they would retain control of the northwest lands or hand them over to the provinces. Finally, in 1905, the government decided to retain control of these lands, the matter was pressed on their attention again, and it took us three years to get this scrip issued. Meantime, the volunteers had lost heart, they had no notion that they were likely to get this scrip, and when at last the minister did justice in the case, or a certain degree of justice, and decided to issue this scrip, the announcement came upon the volunteers so suddenly that, not having saved up their money, they were not in a position to go out and take up their homesteads. I know many volunteers who, if they had had any notion that they were going to get even one year's extension, would not have sold their scrip. The matter was taken up by a number of speculators!, gentlemen who are well known to us, and some of whom are not more than a thousand miles away from this House, they have secured this scrip practically for a song, for a dollar or a dollar and a half per acre, and they retailed it, in many instances, at two and three times what it cost them. I maintain that it is unfair to the volunteer who sold his scrip under the conditions laid down by the old Act that the speculator, who secured that scrip, should have the right to this extension. He will only stand in the way of the honest volunteer who wants to secure a homestead. I maintain that this extension should only be given with respect to scrip already issued to bona fide volunteers who wish to settle on the land themselves. Had they been given the right to take this scrip in 1902, and had they been allowed until 1911 to settle on the land, 95 per cent of the volunteers would have gone upon the land. Had they known that they would have six ur eight years to get ready for settlement upon the land they would have gone upon the land, and would to-day as farmers be assisting in the up-building of the Northwest. As it is the
scrip has largely fallen into the hands of speculators, and I very much fear that the result of one year's extension-I certainly would have preferred two years-will be to cause this scrip still further to fall into the hands of speculators.

I would like to ask the minister whether the class of persons to be benefited by volunteer scrip is to be extended to others. The Imperial South African Volunteer Association, I understand, have applied for a grant. Is it the intention of the government to extend this grant to those persons or to any others who served during the war?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As I have already explained, the Bill simply provides for an extension of time during which the scrip which was provided for under the Act of 1908 may be located. That is the only important provision of the Bill. It does not provide for any extension of the principles of the Act of' 1908, or give the benefit of the Act to any other persons than those provided for in the Act of 1908.

I understand that one hon. gentleman on the other side of the House introduced a motion or a Bill into the House permitting volunteers who had taken up their land and found the land worthless to exchange it for better land elsewhere. I would like to ask the minister if this Bill covers the point, and if it is the intention to grant such a privilege. I understand that quite a number of the volunteers went to the Northwest in good faith to locate their land. They had very little money, and less time. Immediately they landed there they were in the hands of men who were interested in townsites, and land corporations, and they were led off into desert country, in some cases thirty and forty miles away from the railway, and were induced to locate on this land in order to increase the value of other land held by these corporations. After locating, they discovered that their land was of very little use, and in addition that it would be perhaps years before they would be in a position to take advantage of the market being so far away from the railway. One of the hon. members from the west introduced a measure to correct that, and to permit them to exchange their homesteads for other lands more suitable to their purpose. I would like to know if the minister has included a provision in the Bill to meet cases of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Again I have to say that on the introduction of the Bill I stated its provisions. The Bill does not make any provision for the case which my hon. friend has mentioned.

Will there be another Bill introduced that will?

500C

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that, but I presume there will not.

I am sorry to hear the minister state that there are not going to be any extensions or privileges granted to others than those already mentioned in the old Act. In my opinion, Sir, there should be included in the bounty Act the men who enlisted and started on the journey to South Africa, but who met with misfortune of some kind on the way and had to be invalided. I think these invalided men have just as good a right to the privileges as those who went forward and served in the war.
Once they were enlisted.
Yes, I refer to the enlisted men. If there are any changes made in the Act these men should be included in it.

I am very anxious to see this Bill get before the House for the simple reason that I have already introduced a Bill providing that a volunteer or his substitute who had located a warrant on poor land should be able to exchange it. Owing to the position of my Bill on the order paper I have no hope of its being reached this session, but I expect to be able to submit my proposal to the House in the form of an amendment to the Bill which the minister has now introduced. There are only a limited number of men interested in this, but it is a matter of very great importance to each of them, and I hope nothing will happen to interfere with this Bill being submitted to the House so that I may endeavour to incorporate the provisions 6f my Bill in it.

The civil surgeons who went to South Africa and participated in the war and went through all the hardships of the campaign, are deserving of recognition from Canada, and yet they have been denrived of the privileges given to the South African veterans. This matter has been drawn to the attention of the Minister of the Interior on a number of occasions, but so far he has refused to include civil surgeons in this legislation. No more deserving class participated in that campaign, and I would urge that the minister should recognize their services under this Bill.

I endorse what the last speaker has said with regard to the civil surgeons who served in South Africa. What I rise specially for is to ask the Minister of the Interior whether those men who are entitled to land under the Act will be allowed to enter for lands in the Dominion railway belt in British Columbia. I understood the minister to say last year that this would be done, and I wish to know if he has provided for it in this Bill. I Mr. 3. A. CURRIE.
would also ask the minister whether he considers that men who enlisted and who after the war domiciled in Canada are not almost equally entitled with those who were domiciled in Canada at the time of enlistment. I understood the minister to say last session that one object of the Bill was to reward service in the field, and the other object was to secure desirable settlers, and if the Bill has that double purpose I would ask the minister to say whether or not he has considered the claim upon the Dominion of those who were not domiciled in Canada at the time of enlistment, but who became domiciled in Canada after the war. They, like the others, served their country, and they, like the others, would make desirable settlers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Again I have to say that the Bill contains only one provision of im-nortance, and that provision extends the time during which the holders of scrip may locate upon lands in the prairie provinces.
But the minister is open to conversion with regard to these other matters.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the Bill gets into committee that will be the proper time to discuss all these and other suggestions. As to the point raised by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Cowan) that I promised that provision would be made for the location of these grants within the railway belt, I may say that I have no authority to make such a promise. The limitations of the Act as it passed parliament did not permit of that privilege, and the Bill now before parliament does not in its present form provide for it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I notice that I am reported in the newspaper ' Le Canada ' of March 9 as having made a speech in this House yesterday on the navy question, and as having announced myself opposed to the government policy. This must be a typographical error, and I am sorry that it occurred, and I am sure that the gentleman whose name should appear instead of mine will feel equally sorry. As this article is in French, I am unable to read it, but I wish to say that I have not yet made a speech on the navy question, nor had I intended to do so; for I had thought that the matter was tho-

roughly threshed out by men as competent as I am, and perhaps more so. At this point I will only say that I am thoroughly in accord with the government policy. I believe it to be the only policy to be pursued in this young country of ours, to maintain unity amongst all the nationalities that we have in the country, and those that are coming to the country.
The navy question is not before the Chair.
I am perfectly willing to leave it at that.

I wish to ask the Minister of Public Works whether it is true, as announced in the press, that subsidies have been granted for the construction of a dry-dock at Port Arthur, and if so, when it was granted.

House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the second reading of Bill (No. 95), respecting the naval service of Canada, the proposed amendment of Mr. Borden thereto, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Monk.

Mr. Speaker, I think any Ron. member who has had the privilege of being present here during the past two weeks must have realized that if the country is not tired with the discussion of this navy question, the House is absolutely and wholly tired out with it. Last night I made

a good resolution, which I hope I may be able to carry out to the full, that was, that if my remarks had any virtue at all, it would be particularly in the line of brevity. In aproaching the consideration of so great a question as that involved in the motion, and the amendments thereto now under discussion, fraught as it is with 3ueh vast possibilities to the future history and destiny of Canada, I do so with a good deal of timidity, and trepidity as well. Having listened carefully to the debate, and having read the speeches when I have not been permitted to hear them, I am conscious that in many respects I do not concur either in the amendment to the amendment, or in the amendment, and that I am not wholly in accord with the original motion itself. Although I think I can fairly say that I am not wholly discordant with the principles and spirit which that notion breathes, but am wholly out of tune with the propositions involved in the amendment to the amendment, and the amendment to the motion. So emphatic is this realization that I begin to be impressed with the conviction that I shall be obliged, like Lobd Dundreary's peacock, to flock all by myself alone. For thirty-five years and upwards I have been an active adherent of the Liberal party, I am so today, and I believe that I shall be to the moment of drawing my latest breath. For thirty-five years I have served that party, and I hope that a few years more at least will be permitted me to continue that service. One of the reasons why I have been associated with the Liberal party, 'and why I hope to be continued with it, is the liberty of conscience that is given to every individual member of the party. That has been the history of the party in the past, and the moment that it deviates from that course, it will have ceased to be a Liberal party.
Now, Sir, I am making these remarks for a very good reason. I have said that I am not in perfect accord with the Bill which is involved in the original motion, and I hope before I take my seat to explain wherein that is the case. It is not pleasant for one who has been a great many years a follower of that party to find himself unable to see eye to eye with it, yet there are occasions in the life of every public man when his convictions must not be suppressed, when they should not be submerged, and I simply propose to state before this House and the country the views which I hold on this great question. I have said that it involves the future destiny and history of this Dominion. I go further and say that it involves the present conditions under which we are living. I go still further and say that it is a momentous question, involving almost every condition of public service, and every idea with respect to the course and

administration of government. Holding that view it is but fair that, since I cannot accept all that those with whom I have been associated desire to have adopted, I should explain my position, not only to my friends, but to the House and to the country at large. I have the greatest confidence in the leaders of the Liberal party, and I regret that I have not, perhaps, the same confidence in my own judgment. I may be absolutely and entirely wrong, but I am bound to be true to my own convictions, regardless whether my judgment be good or the reverse. The convictions I hold are honest and sincere, and as such I must stand by them.
No one listening to this debate could fail to be impressed with two prominent features which have characterized it. First, the desire of those who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, to demonstrate the glorious inconsistency and variableness of those who sit on your left; and I am bound to say that the attempt has been crowned with a measure of success, somewhat startling, if not wholly edifying and comforting to the people of Canada. The second feature is the determined effort of those who sit on your left, Sir, to prove to the world at large that those who sit on your right are absolutely enemies of the empire, traitors to His Majesty the King, his crown and realm and# person, and to the flag which heretofore, in our enthusiasm, we have been proud to say has braved the battle and the breeze throughout the lifetime of the British nation. All this is an edifying spectacle indeed. As regards the effort to prove inconsistency, even if inconsistency be proved up to the hilt, and out of the very mouths of the offenders, is it really germane to the problem we are attempting to solve by the agency of this Bill? True it may not be flattering to this country to have it shown that the leaders of a great party, bent on securing the reins of government, are simply playing the role of opportunists, and are as variable and mercurial as an April day, regardless of the country's peril or the people's interest. But that question is one which the party leaders will have to settle with their followers and the country at a later day. Such a spectacle presented in this day and generation may tend to shake public confidence in the men who essay to govern and thereby become the guardians of the political and national conscience of Canada, but it does not greatly illumine the subject to be dealt with. Of one thing it does convince us, and that is that there is room in Canada for a Canadian James Russell Lowell, and a Canadian Hosea Bigelow to illustrate the characteristics of our political conditions at this time.
The other attempt which has been made has been to show that those who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, are disloyal. That is a very old cry. It is one with which we
are all familiar, and is certainly not one upon which I should claim the attention of this House at any length. I have heard that cry from the very beginning of my knowledge of political affairs. I have heard it raised against the Liberal party. In my boyhood days, particularly after the struggle for responsible government in Nova Scotia, I heard that great statesman, Joseph Howe, denounced as disloyal, and as an innovator, not true to his King and country, because he contended for a larger measure of freedom and political control in the affairs of the country in which he lived. This cry has always been the answer to those who were pleading for an enlargement of the people's rights. When there is nothing else to be said against any one or against any political party, the attempt is made to prove disloyalty. Now, while I hold the views I do with respect to this subject, I do not think it is fair to say of the right hon. gentleman who introduced this Bill (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that he is in any sense disloyal, or that he is not as sincere is his desire for the advancement of the country as any other hon. member in this House. It is not fair to say that one party has a monopoly of loyalty, and of a desire to advance the interests of the country; and I think that we can sweep away as unworthy of our consideration all arguments advanced with a view to show either inconsistency on the part of the Conservative party or disloyalty on the part of the Liberal party, in the consideration of this question.
Now, Sir, I will reverse the order of the motions in my consideration of them. First, I will consider the amendment to the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk); then the amendment to the original motion which was moved by the hon. leader of the opposition; and lastly, the original motion involving the adop tion of the Bill introduced by the right hon. the Prime Minister. Now, as to the policy involved in the amendment to the amendment, I can best characterize it as a ' do-nothing policy.' We remember that in the United States, many years ago, they had what was called a ' know-nothing policy '-and' I suppose my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier is the leader of a third party in this country which advocates a ' do-nothing policy.' I have no sympathy with the ideas involved in that amendment to the amendment; while I have every respect, indeed a pro found respect, for the hon. gentleman himself, who stands well in this House and in this country, a man of culture, a man of broad ideas, a man of ability. I respect him as such, but I certainly think that he has not done justice either to himself, or to Canada, which he, in common with the rest of us, I hope, loves, or to
5C07

Great Britain, to which he gives a great deal of credit.
The next in order for consideration is the amendment moved by the hon. leader of the opposition. That seems t-o me to be based on two principles, one, that of a contribution called for by- an emergency . crisis, and the other, the policy of a plebiscite. Now, I shall endeavour to deal with this amendment from the standpoint of a contribution, I do not propose to discuss at any length the question of a crisis, or an emergency. That has been treated so fully that I think we may consider it as having been disposed of, so far as it enters into a discussion of this question. As to that amendment advocating a contribution. it cannot be said that it is anything more than an act of expediency, not one of policy. No hon. gentleman can say that, so far as that amendment relates to the contribution of Dreadnoughts, it lays down a platform or a policy for the people of Canada to follow. It might, under certain circumstances, be considered as a generous act; it might, if you will, be considered as a quid pro quo offered in a moment of magnaminity. But it can never be said that it contains a policy for the people of Canada to build upon, a platform upon which they can start out to erect their superstructure. We must remember that we have to deal with this question, not merely for the present but for the future, and that as we start to build, so will the completion of our structure be. If there is anything in the idea of the amendment, it is in my judgment foreign to the spirit of the government under which we live. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in his boyhood days, I know, was wont to pay great attention to the public speeches, lectures and utterances of the late Hon. Joseph Howe; and I fancy there is no gentleman sitting in this Chamber who is more familiar with the utterances of that great statesman. I know that he must have a clear memory of the speeches that gentleman delivered at Southampton, of the letters to Earl Grey, to Sir Francis Hincks, the twelve resolutions which he moved early in the history of colonial government in Nova Scotia, and his great speeches on the organization of the empire. My hon. friend, brought up, as I know he was, and as 1 was, in a Liberal family, must have been familiar with the principles which the Hon. Joseph Howe enunciated; and I am sure that when my hon. friend came to pen that amendment he must have felt that he was contradicting every principle and all the early teachings concerning responsible government which he had imbibed from that great statesman. For that reason I would dispose, so far as I am Mr. EMMEESON.
individually concerned, of that amendment as unsatisfactory; I could not find it in my heart to vote in favour of it. I repudiate the idea that we are mere colonists, I repudiate the terms 'colony' and 'colonists'. They may have been proper terms to use in the early days when we were a Crown colony, when, we were looking to Downing street, when we were mere subjects, subservient to a government beyond the sea; but to-day we stand in an entirely different position.
How?

To-day we have local responsible self-government within Canada and within the provinces of Canada and so we should have a reasonable respect for our surroundings, for our conditions, for our rights, for our dignity as a young nation within the great empire of Great Britain.
As to the second feature, that of the plebiscite, it does not occur to me as necessary that this matter should be submitted to the people of Canada. We must all recognize that this question has not been entirely overlooked. The attitude taken by the government of Canada in 1902 and in 1907, has my fullest and heartiest support. I also support in its entirety the principle contained in the resolution of March 29, 1909, the point where I diverge from it being as to its inclusion of the word speedy, and the meaning of this I shall explain later. I have said that the principles enunciated by the government in 1902, 1907 and 1909 have my approval and concurrence and I shall endeavour to show how these principles can best be turned into effect, having regard to the conditions prevailing in Canada and to the future of this country. I have endeavoured to express the idea that the amendment of the leader of the opposition does not contain a policy but simply a suggestion as to an expedient and it is not I think, worthy of any great party that seeks to administer the affairs of Canada. Its whole foundation, if it has any reason for existence at all, lies in the attempted creation of a German scare,, of a menace to the empire of Britain, from the German or some other empire. Such a menace, it seems to me, does not exist. We have had many scares in this country originating under conditions not unlike these. The entrance of New Brunswick to confederation resulted because of a Fenian scare. Later we have had the Russian scare, we have had the French scare. All these were great crises. Later on we have had many election scares, we have had the scare of French domination in our province and all over the Dominion. These scares and these fancied crises originate, I was almost going to say from brains that are sprained in some way, they are not merely the result of brain storms I but they are spasms and paroxysms that

seem to come to political parties at intervals and at times when there is some great end to serve and some great purpose to achieve. Therefore I say that in so far as the basis for any contribution is concerned, it is gone and absolutely gone, as has been demonstrated to this House time and again in the last few days by the extracts quoted from the speeches of prominent men in Great Britain, of the chancellor of the German empire, and the utterances of a few days ago of the great thunderer of Great Britain, the London ' Times.1 It is conceded on all sides that there is no emergency, that there is no crisis, that it simply exists as a conjuring of the brain. Assuming that it does not exist, then where falls this policy of a contribution. England does not want it, she does not ask it. What England wants is some assertion of principle and policy on the part of the Canadian people that will be a moral force in support of the empire and that will be a notification to the nations of the world that if Great Britain is in trouble, if the empire of Britain is menaced or imperilled, the dominions beyond the seas will be at her back and will spend their money, their men and their strength without stint. I believe that if a national crisis existed, Canada would give money and men without stint. But does the emergency exist? There is no one who can say it does exist or that there is a likelihood of its existence and therefore it is simply now a question for this House and this country to consider as to the course that Canada should take in connection with her attitude as a young nation within the great mother nation of the empire.
This leads me to the consideration of the original motion, the one to the effect that we shall have the second reading of this Bill and go into Committee of the Whole to take into consideration what we should do towards helping the empire, not merely in a crisis or in the event of a crisis but as a settled policy, a policy whereby we shall be recognized measureably as a part of the British empire, at least sustaining the burdens and assisting in the protection of ourselves as a portion of the empire and aiding and contributing to the support and the defence of the empire at large. It is simply a question, after all, as to the means to an end. I would like to deal with the practical and economic features of this measure. I would stop to analyse for a moment Canada's position in respect to the empire and with respect to the conditions prevailing within her own bounds. What is expedient for her, using the word expedient with its wide and proper meaning. It is a question of expediency, having Tegard to our conditions, having regard to our situation, having regard to the problems which we have in hand at this time, and which we anticipate having in hand in 159
the near future. In determining that question of expediency we must not forget that everybody's problem in life is not to fancy what he would like to do but to find out what he has to do and make the very best that he can of it. What is thus true of the individual is true in the larger sense of nationhood. Now, the Bill involved in the motion of the right hon. leader of the government is one that is worthy of consideration. Let me say at the very outset that I have always agreed and do now agree with the principle of that Bill. I question its necessity at this moment. I question the judgment that would conclude that it was necessary to introduce it before the people of Canada at this moment, but that is merely my opinion and I hope always to have the courage of those opinions born of conviction and sincerity.
Now, I want to make a little personal explanation. I have been credited with the coinage of a term that has been freely circulated from one end of this country to the other. I refer to the phrase ' a tin-pot navy.' Let me say that if there is any credit for the coinage of a phrase, I am not entitled to any credit for the coining of that phrase. More than that, I am not aware that I ever made use of such a term I know that I never voiced the words, and yet I am told that this was given free circulation in some of the public newspapers in Canada. If I had used the term, I would stand by it, but as I did not, I must relinquish claim to the credit and repudiate this as an utterance by me. But, Mr. Speaker, we must realize in dealing with this measure the conditions under which we are living to-day. Canada has many great transportation problems. The extension of our canal system and the creation and construction of magnificent railways are necessary to the development of our rapidly expanding country. The deepening and widening of our waterways, the extension of our trade abroad, the establishment, in the interests of the people of this Dominion, of commercial agencies wherever there is trade to be had, the initiation of a policy which would have, as representatives of this Dominion in every country where Canada has trade, agents of our Customs Department in order that they might spy! out the opportunities and report the conditions affecting the internal affairs of Canada, our tariff conditions and our trade, to our government, which reports could be disseminated through the country to the advantage of the commercial world and the business element which are becoming so prominent within our borders-these are all great problems that must be solved. We must also recognize that we have assumed immense burdens, that we have taken hold of difficulties that to greater countries, and countries of greater wealth, would be recog-

nized as almost insurmountable. We have one great transcontinental railway, and we have two others in course of construction, and both nearing completion. The people of the country to the south of us, although they have a population of upwards of eighty millions, although they have been in advance of 'us in the business and industrial world, have not one single transcontinental line of railway spanning their country from the shores of the Atlantic to the shores of the Pacific. That is a startling fact, but it is one that is true, nevertheless. They possess railways connecting one with the other whereby you can start from the Pacific ocean and reach the Atlantic, but they have never assumed the burdens in connection with transcontinental railways which the people of Canada have had the* courage to undertake. We want, in addition to that, to bring about the development of our transportation facilities. We want population. Canada wants more steamship services from the St. Lawrence and the maritime ports, to every port in the world. She wants to enlarge and deepen -her canals and improve her river channels so as to accommodate the largest ships. She requires the construction of new canals, new railways and branch lines for those railways. Then, these branch lines must connect sections wherever population is to be found with the centres of population. She wants these lines projected into- every section where a mining or agricultural population can be maintained. She demands large expenditures, not only in furthering a great national policy of transportation, but also in promoting the increase of her population. The people want a live, up-to-date and intelligent grasp of the necessities of the hour, with hustling action on the part of governments and those charged with the responsibility of the development of the country. They do not want, timid hesitancy in respect to these matters. The prophecy of the right hon. leader of the government that the twentieth century would be Canada's will be realized if we are but measureably active and alert with regard to the illimitable and rich natural resources of our country.
These are some of the wants of Canada. We are face to face with meeting, those wants, and in that connection comes up the question of the advisability of the construction of a navy at the present time. Well, Sir, I do not take very great exception to the initial cost, either of the commencement or the completion of a navy in itself. But, one must bear in mind that we are embarking on a wider sea than, these limitations would indicate. There is the question of the maintenance of that navy, and as to that I shall not refer particularly. What I want this parliament to remember is that in the adoption of this Bill we must Mr. EMMERSON.
be careful not to overlook the fact that if you have a navy to defend your coasts you must have in conjunction with it modem fortifications in every sea-port, and harbour on the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans, and so, when we embark on the construction of a navy we are of necessity launched into immense expenditure for these fortifications. The question then comes for our consideration, are we in a position to assume the burden in the manner proposed? As an incident of a navy we must have dockyards, we must have dry-docks, and I suppose we must have admiralty boards and councils. I am no pessimist with respect to the strength, and the willingness, and the power of the Canadian people to accomplish great undertakings. I believe that our people are able to overcome any difficulty that is likely in the ordinary course of events to confront them, but, we are charged with the responsibility of legislating, and we must hesitate before we place burdens upon the people. I am not now speaking of the proposal in this Bill as a contrast to what has been proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition. His proposal means a grant of $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 offhand, and the proposal of the right hon. the Prime Minister means not so many millions at the outset, but it involves great incidental expenditures which may be, and will be in my judgment an obligation upon the Canadian people for all time to come. Then, let us ask ourselves if this navy in one form or other is a necessity at this moment. And, Sir, in considering that question, while I defer to the judgment of the right hon. gentleman, and of those by whom he is surrounded in council, I do say that the spasm and the paroxysm that has seized upon hon. gentlemen opposite in their clamouring for a contribution, and for Dreadnoughts ad libitum to be sent across the water has impregnated _ the atmosphere to some extent although it seems to have lost some of its power in its passage across the floor. However, there is not a difference as to principle, it is simply a difference as to detail, Now, Mr. Speaker, I may say that the expenditure foT maintaining the proposed navy, and for the continuance of admiralty boards and councils is, perhaps, not an obstacle that should frighten the people. But, when we realize that Canada has expended in the last twenty years for the maintenance of our militia upwards of $60,000,000 we can form some estimate of what the establishment of a navy, and naval boards, and naval councils will mean. I may be somewhat radical on these points; it may be that I have not a due appreciation of the requirements of this country, but I have felt that already we have had too much of these military councils; that we have had entirely

too much of men going from one end of the country to the other, who toil not and neither do they spin, and yet none are arrayed like one of these, and who have placed in their hands, by the influence of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as well as on this, thousands and hundreds of thousands, and millions of dollars year after year to sustain this great establishment. And, Sir, when I realize what that expenditure would have done in other directions, I confess that I am sorry it has not been spent in what to me would appear a manner more conducive to the welfare of our country. I am no lover of post mortem examinations into the past, but I feel it my duty to invite the attention of the House to that expenditure in order that we may realize in some degree what may be expected from us in the future if we duplicate these organizations in the form of a navy, and navy boards, and naval councils-Lord high admirals and admirals, and so on. Now, Sir, I can read the condition of Canada to-day in the light of history. When the thirteen colonies declared for independence they had terrible difficulties to surmount in the matter of their maritime power, and the success which attended an earnest sincere, and valiant people was little dreamed of by Lord North, and those who inspired him at the beginning of that struggle. I can come down further in the light of the history of the war of 1812, and realize what an effieient navy meant to the American union at the time of the declaration of that war. Although the union had been preparing for that conflict she had not more than seventeen war vessels, but she had a splendid merchant marine which was found to be an efficient auxiliary to the naval force, and which in a very short time was supplied with 50,000 men. The union did not have more than six warships proper, and these were frigates of no large size, manned by 5,000 sailors. I may be told that conditions have changed, and so they have. But, Sir, although I have spoken longer than I intended, I must continue in order to say that I would have been glad if the government could have presented a Bill containing the very principles which this Bill contains, but also containing suggestions which I shall with all due deference place before the House, and especially submit for the consideration of hon. gentlemen opposite as a restraining influence upon their frenzied brain style of reaching forward towards Dreadnoughts ad libitum.
I would have been glad if the government had introduced a measure providing for training ships in sufficient number to meet the requirements of the Atlantic sea-board, the Pacific sea-board and the inland waters of Canada, the great lakes. Training 1591
ships to do what? To furnish the personnel for a navy that must come. If we are to reach out into greater nationhood, if we are to expand and develop, if our population is to increase, it is not so very far in the future where, without regard to any condition that may exist elsewhere, but as a necessity of our internal conditions, our growth and expansion, there will be a necessity for the establishment of a navy suitable to our means and our conditions. That training could provide, first, somewhat on the lines of the Newfoundland naval reserve, a scheme to educate the seamen of the east and of the west and along the lakes, so that they would graduate into a navy almost automatically. We must remember that in the manning of a navy conditions have changed from what they were in 1812 and in 1775. To-day it is not merely able-bodied seamen and men of valour that are required; Out you want technically trained men; you want the machinist, the mechanic, the electrical engineer. You want men with trained eyes and trained hands and trained brains, and they cannot be created in a day. They are the condition precedent ot a navy; and I would add, and I think the people of Canada would add and demand, that when we have a navy it should be Canadian-built and Canadian-manned. And what is more, I never want to see a ship of the naval force of Canada launched into the waters of our coasts commanded by any other than a Canadian or controlled by any but men of our own Canadian brain and brawn. That would be my idea. Correlative with that I would provide for an emergency. I would have that training fleet in operation, and I would begin to provide for what might be termed a peace fund in Canada-a fund that could be changed into a fund, if necessity arose, for the protection of the empire. Now, why have such a fund? Canada can, it is true, stand, and would be willing to stand, large contributions for her own development and for the defence of the empire. We all recognize and gratefully acknowledge the fact that our trade routes and our commerce are protected by the navy of England. In proportion to our trade and in proportion to the protection given to it, our customs revenues expand and increase; they are expanding and increasing year by year; and the people of Canada would do right, and they would be willing to do it, to set aside year by year a percentage of those customs revenues-it might amount to $3,000,000 or $5,000,000 or more each year; and the fund so formed could be placed, if you will, to the credit of Canada in the bank of England, and named, if it needed a name, 'Canada's peace fund.' It would be a notification to the nations of Europe and to the world that Canada was determined to

support the empire in her hour of need, if that hour ever came. That fund would grow. In the meantime, it would cost nothing to maintain. There would be no outgoes in the maintenance of it, and it would be ready at any moment, if the emergency arose, and could be contributed at once to the empire for the benefit of the empire. Is there anything more needed by a nation in stress of conflict than money? Recent l istory has demonstrated that. The war between Russia and Japan and the war between Spain and the United States are illustrations. Even in the Boer war Great Britain did not find it very easy to provide the funds to enable her to put down the Boers. Votes of money were given, and given generously and freely; but the burden on the people of Great Britain was very great. The additions to the budget were enormous, but they were cheerfully assumed by the people of Great Britain. But if in case of an emergency we were in a position to place at the disposal of the empire 950,000,000, or $40,000,000, or $30,-000,00J, this would certainly be a contribution that would be of advantage, and would demonstrate to the world that we were doing something in support of the empire, even if we did not send Dreadnoughts. What, Sir, would such legislation mean? After all, what was wanted by Great Britain was a declaration on the part of the overseas dominions that would have a moral effect with the nations of tne world; and if it were known by Germany or any other European nation that Canada was preparing a fund primarily for the preservation of peace-because, after all, as I understand it, these armaments are justified because they tend to preserve the peace of the world-consider the moral effect the knowledge of such a fact would have. At least that is how the nations justify the creation of great naval fleets and the establishment of great armaments. They plead that they are incurring these heavy expenditures in order that the peace of the world may be preserved, il an enactment by Canada would not be a notification to ail these nations that Great Britain would have our support, I do not know of any other course that could more effectively convey that idea. I shall not touch upon the fact that the United States and Japan have lessened their war appropriations at the verv moment when we are proposing to launch out into this heavy expenditure. Japan, in its last estimates, decreased its vote for the navy and army, and so did the United States, whereas we in Canada are going to branch out into an increased expenditure this year and a still greater expenditure next year.
I could not divest myself of my personal responsibility even if I would. I owe a duty to my constituents, and I recognize Mr. EMMERSON.
the fact that I am absolutely and unreservedly opposed to the policy of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) and also to the do-nothing policy of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). Then what shall I support? I shall take a course without fear, favour or affection, and I assume that every hon. gentleman will do the same. But I find myself, as I have said, very much in the position of Lord Dundreary's peacock. I am obliged to flock all by myself alone, but there is a bird near me which is more to my own liking. I cannot have what I would. All government is based on compromise. We cannot all have our own way, and I have given this matter great consideration. I am bound to say that there has not been any man on either side who has asked me wdiat my attitude was on this question. My declaration by my vote will be in favour of the principle which I have enunciated-that is a principle which involves a policy which is Canadian, which is for the future, and which means something for the empire. To give a contribution this year or next year to Great Britain would mean perhaps that we would be expected to do that the following year, but there would be no fixed understanding. One government and one parliament might do it, and another might not. But to put it in a form of an enactment, showing what Canada is prepared to do, is a tangible something which governments and parliaments cannot violate, which would go on for the benefit of the empire and the advantage of Canada, particularly as I see it. I did not intend to take up so much of the time of the House. I have given criticisms on the details of the Bill which perhaps would have been more opportune in Committee of the Whole; but its principles are quite in accord with my own and the scheme proposed is in a sense identical with my views except in this respect, that I say the time has not come for us to launch it. My hon. friends say: yes, it has. My hon. friends opposite say send millions and send Dreadnoughts; do that without plebiscites, but do not do the other without going back home and consulting the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
speechtext:
I do not intend to weary the House by following the argument, if it may be so called, of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Emmer-son), further than to congratulate him upon being, as he assures us he is, the only member of this House, amongst two hundred odd, who has not gone into paroxisms and spasms on this question. While he was making his plea, one would have thought that his argument would have lead to the very reverse of the conclusion

he arrived at. The hon. gentleman compared himself to the historical peacock. I should have thought that he would have added another bird to his aviary and would more fittingly have likened himself to a peacock of canabalistic propensities with a dish of crow before it which it was eating with undoubted enjoyment. The hon. gentleman has given us reason after reason why the Bill of the government should not pass, and he consequently felt impelled to state that no doubt we would be surprised to find that after all he was supporting the government. Well, speaking for myself, I was not at all surprised. I had no idea that he would do anything else except eat crow. I was therefore not at all surprised that, after making a speech bristling with declarations of independence, he should wind up by supporting the government. He still, however, tries to leave the House in some doubt as to what he may do in the end, because he still reserves the right to bring forward in committee a do-nothing policy of his own. He is not going to do this, that, or the other thing. He does not approve of the government policy, he cannot vote for that of the leader of the opposition, and he is very much incensed at the policy introduced by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, which he styles a do-nothing policy, and he winds up by declaring, what no one doubted, that he would support the government, taking care, however, to throw out some obscure intimations as to some [DOT] other course which he may take during the debate in committee.
The main reason why he opposes the policy of the leader of the opposition is that, first of all, there is no emergency, and secondly, that he wants the people of this country to understand that the proposal of the opposition is not one of policy, but of expediency. Let me ask the hon. gentleman: Can he name to me a wiser, a higher quality of policy for this great country than the declaration to the world at large that any nation which interferes with the mother country will at the same time interfere with Canada? I see that the hon. gentleman has gone out. Will some one kindly ask him to come back before the debate closes, because 1 would like to put to him this question; and I would use my influence- with my party and try to prevail on the leader of the government to allow the rules to be broken end give the hon. gentleman another opportunity to speak on this question, and tell us, if he can, what policy would be grander, nobler or better for the country than one by which Canada would declare, not only to Germany, but the world ai large, that, in case of emergency, no matter how many millions were required, Canada would stand by the mother country first,
last and all the time. The hon. gentleman, throughout his remarks, indicated that he was in favour of British connection, but if there is anything in his so-called flocking alone policy, it means that Canada should go meandering along, taking the benefit all through the ages of everything that Great Britain has done for this country in the way of constructing a navy for the advantage of the trade of Canada to enable us to produce, as we all want to do, flourishing manufactories, with the means of shipping our wheat to foreign countries, and doing all this while sponging on Great Britain to protect our products while we send them forth into the universe. My hon.- friend talked about dignity; my hon. friend talked, I took down his words, about a ' dignified policy for Canada.' Well, now, I would not like to give my boys a lesson upon dignity in the sense that the hon gentleman understands dignity. I would not like a boy of mine, after I had educated him and fitted him for a successful career in life, after I had taught him lessons of manliness, and endeavoured to instil in his heart a love of uprightness and nobility, nationally as well as individually, after I had done all this for him, and after he had grown up to manhood, I would not think it would be dignified for him to say to his father: I am 21 years of age, and the old man is 65, -and it is dignified in me to repudiate him if I can save a little money by so doing. The hon. member may consider that dignity in the county of Westmorland, but my constituents would call it gross meanness.
He talks about the meaning of the word ' speedy.' He voted for that resolution, which the leader of the opposition put forward as an amendment in order to save the honour of this country by giving speedy relief; and the hon. gentleman, forsooth, wants to beat around the upper lakes with a few fishing boats, and still he does not make up his mind what kind of a flag they are to sail under. And he does not want to do even this for five, ten or fifteen years. Sir, I must say that his opinion of what is speedy relief is entirely at variance with the idea of an ordinary school boy, let alone a grown up person in the county of Lincoln. But just as the hon. gentleman wants to do his duty to his constituents, so I am bound to say, in doing my duty to my constituents, that that is not my view of what constitutes speedy relief to the motherland.
Now, the hon. gentleman pooh poohed the idea that there was any emergency. The hon. gentleman has a colleague here from his province in the person of the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) who declared, as he was bound to declare, the other day, in my hearing, and in this same debate, that he did not

agree with the contention of the other government supporters that there was no emergency; he made a very powerful argument to show that there is an emergency, and that this country requires something to be done in order that Great Britain may understand our position in that emergency. So, while the hon. member for Westmorland is trying to walk alone, he is up against the arguments of a gentleman on his own side of the House, as well as against the arguments of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. Having said this much in criticism of the hon. gentleman's speech, I need not bother this House any more with him.	. .
Now, as to the Bill itself, what position are we in? The government admits, by the introduction of this Bill, that something has got to be done.
Now, the whole issue between us is.: Are we to deal with Canada alone, or with Canada as a part of the British empire? That is the crux of the question, and we must facv it. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you realize that as well as any other hon. member in this House-must we consider Canada as an independent nation, or as a part of the British empire? The hon. gentleman no doubt is sincere in the stand he takes. I do not say that in any sneering manner, because I believe that hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere, although they may forget themselves on occasions. But I apprehend that hon. gentlemen supporting the government are sincere when they say that there is no emergency, and that consequently we should shape our course as though Great Britain did not need our assistance. For my part I believe that there is an emergency, and even the government supporters admit that if there were an emergency it would be the duty of Canada to render effectual assistance to the empire. However, they deny the existence of the emergency and hope that no emeregency will ever occur, although we fear it will. Now, if they are sincere when they argue in thi3 manner, it does seem strange to me that they have not seen a way out of the difficulty. If they are sincere, why do they not adopt the amendment of the leader of the opposition and so relieve themselves from the difficulty? Let them adopt the amendment of the leader of the opposition if they are desirous of maintaining the integrity of the British empire, and every one of their views will be complied with. If there is not an emergency, they will still be showing their adhesion to the view that Canada is an integral part of the British empire, and is bound to do something for imperial defence; while if there is an emergency, they are rendering that speedy assistance to the mother country which the resolution of last March calls for. Sir, it is not the paltry value of the money gift Mr. LANCASTER.
that counts in this matter, but it is the great moral influence which Canada will exert upon the whole world by taking her stand by the side of the mother country. Every hon. gentleman on that side of the House assumes in his argument that if Great Britain were attacked it would be wise and right for Canada to stand at her back.	,
Now, I appeal, if it is not too late, to the Prime Minister himself. Could _he not call his supporters together again in caucus and say to them: Gentlemen, I gather from the arguments of those of you who have spoken on this question that it is very desirable that the parliament of Canada should be united, and as the amendment of the leader of the opposition meets the objections of the member for Westmorland, as it does not propose any permanent tax upon the people of this country, as it does not propose the adoption of a naval policy until the question has been discussed upon the hustings, let us all vote for the amendment of the leader of the opposition. Sir, there can be only one reason why the Prime Minister wont do that, and that reason must be because he is not prepared at all hazards to say that the Canadian fleet, in time of war, must be controlled by the British admiralty. That must be his only reason, because there can be no other. I would not suggest that the right hon. gentleman is not loyal. It is not fair to suggest that hon. gentlemen, his supporters on the other side of the House are not loyal; but it doe3 become fair and right to discuss the question of loyalty when a proposition is made that modifies in any way our constitutional relations to the mother country. It is right to ask whither such a course is tending. Now, I am going at first to discuss this question upon the basis of what is best for us standing alone; and then I will discuss it from the point of view of what we should do as an integral part of the empire.
First of all what have we to gain by having a navy in this country that is not to be controlled by Great Britain, and, again what harm can it do us if our navy is controlled by Great Britain unless, I say again, you are determined to leave the door open for separation instead of locking that door and make sure that you and your descendants for all time will remain British subjects. There is nothing in the amendment of the leader of the opposition that can do the Canadians any harm whatever unless the Canadians are anxious to have the door left open, to have a chance to escape British connection and to become independent. If some hon. gentlemen, as two or three have admitted, are voting for this Bill because it may lead to independence, that of itself seems to me is a reason why the rest of us ought to rise and say: Under the British North America Act we

cannot do that, it is not only illegal but absolutely disloyal in the sense of a breaking of the allegiance which, while the British North America Act continues and this country remains under the constitution, cannot be broken except by rebellion. These hon. gentlemen, it seems to me, are not so much to blame as the Prime Minister who has led the way in regard to this Bill. The Prime Minister undertook to say he was neither an imperialist nor an antiimperialist. With all deference I am bound to say there are some things in this world that must be either yes or no. I cannot believe that I am married to my wife and I am not married to her. I cannot believe that Edward Hamilton Lancaster is my son to-day and reserve the right to say, ten years hence, that he is not my son. I cannot believe that I am free to reserve the right to say I am an imperialist and I am an anti-imperialist. I do not believe that I can owe. allegiance to Great Britain unless I am an imperialist, I cannot see any difference between an oath of allegiance and imperialism. What is allegiance? I am speaking only for myself in what I am going to say. I believe that every gentleman has a right to be guided by his own conscience. I have to be guided by mine and many a time my conscience has caused me to refrain from doing things because I thought them wrong while other men felt free to do those things. It is a matter between the man and his Maker. I have three times taken the oath of allegiance to King Edward. There is nothing in that oath permitting you to change your mind ten or fifteen years hence. Before I was allowed to take my seat in this House I had to take that oath. It is absolute and unalterable, a man taking it swears allegiance to King Edward. I do not see how I am to keep that oath and vote for a Bill which would construct a navy not under King Edward's control if we are to remain a part of the empire. The arguments of hon. gentlemen would tend to the belief that we have reached something which we have not reached. They argue that it is just as well to have an independent Canadian navy. And why? So that they may or may not interfere in wars in which Great Britain may become engaged. The very minute that you establish the principle that a navy built by Canada may or may not, as it sees fit at the time, join the motherland in its wars, that very moment you are proposing a rebelion if that policy is insisted on. Why do I say that? There is the navy constructed, there is the navy ready to fight. An order comes from Ottawa saying whether or not our navy is to join in that war. Suppose it does not join in the war. What is that navy? It is not an imperialist, it is an anti-imperialist. The imperial navy is at war with Germany or Austria, or Russia or some
other country and where is the Canadian navy under those circumstances, what condition is it in? How can any one say that Canada can remain part of the empire and take such a stand as that, it is an absolute contradiction in terms? It is claimed sometimes that a man has a right to fence. I have never thought it wise to fence. Although I have a close constituency which at the time I first ran was supposed to be strongly hostile to my party I have never thought it would pay, I have never dared to insult my constituents, my wife or my children, by undertaking to say both yes and no on any question. A man is no good in my opinion if he cannot find what his duty is under such circumstances. The Prime Minister is in an impossible position when he says he is neither an imperialist nor an anti-imperialist, just as Edward Hamilton Lancaster, must be my son or must not be; it is impossible to say that he may be one day and may not be another day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The right hon. gentleman thinks this is very funny, that it is quite a joke. I am trying to illustrate in a practical way what I understand by my oath of allegiance and by allegiance to any country. It may appear to be very clever to take this double position. Just as it may appear to be clever to denounce the Manitoba school question in Ontario and uphold it in Quebec, so it may appear to be clever to say in some parts of the country: Sir Wilfrid said in the House that he was not an imperialist, and to have 'Hansard' scored out with pencil or with scissors, and to say in another province: The Prime Minister said in the House that he was an imperialist. Thus I say the Prime Minister has set a bad example to his followers and we see the fruits of that example, when he says that he is not an imperialist and not an antiimperialist.
The right hon. gentleman made a quotation which I think was an unfortunate one for him. He quoted Kipling:
Daughter am I in my mother's house,
But mistress in my own.
Daughter in his mother's house? What kind of a daughter? What kind of a good-looking little Canadian girl, I do not care about the English or the Scotch or the Irish girl, but what kind of a little Canadian girl? What about my daughter? -for I have got one-I wish I had a dozen. After her father educates her and teaches her all he can and after her mother teaches her and brings her up to honourable womanhood, suppose that she is given a magnificent fruit farm and is allowed to use it without rent or taxes; suppose some

one comes to her and says: Do you know that your mother and father are being beset by barn burners and others? What kind of a daughter in her mother's house, would she be if she would not give up everything she had to protect the old gentleman and the old lady? Daughter am I in my mother's house-yes, a most unworthy daughter who would have the contempt of the whole world, if under the circumstances of this Bill he did not do what we are advocating. Kipling said both things, daughter in my mother's house and mistress in my own. Mistress in my own? Yes, mistress in Canada, in the autonomy of Canada, in dealing with great transportation questions, in making protective or free trade policies for her farmers, her manufacturers and all her people. Absolute autonomy is what I fight for, absolute autonomy in Canada. Let Canada attend to its own affairs absolutely. Let Great Britain keep its hands off the British North America Act. But the same British North America Act which gives us autonomy in Canada to deal with our domestic affairs has given us no right when we get outside of Canada to interfere with imperial affairs. Daughter in my mother's -house, is not Canada's autonomy. 'Daughter in our ; mother's house' is outside of Canada, it has relation to imperial affairs. Mistress in our own house is dealing with Canada's affairs and this Naval Bill is going beyond Canada's affairs and interfering with imperial' affairs. Under those circumstances I cannot but regret that a gentleman like the hon. gentleman from South Huron is induced to ask in this House: What did Great Britain ever do for us? The poison, so to speak, which was sown upon the second reading of the Bill has reached him. He is a Scotchman, or a gentleman of Scotch descent, and he is a man above all others, perhaps, except an Englishman which I am myself, who would be expected to suggest that these imperial rights should exist in this country. As I am referring to what he said, it is fair to quote his exact language and therefore I would refer the House to page 4520 of 'Hansard'. After saying that Great Britain had done nothing for us, that she never gave us any more for our lard, our oats, our wheat, our cabbage, or something of that kind, than any other country, that she did not give us more than our goods were worth-and I do not know of any Canadian who would be undignified enough to want to get more than his goods were worth-he proceeds to say:
It is quite proper that I should say that our love for and devotion to the mother country is only commencing. Filial affection, I am sure, is one of the noblest traits of human nature; but filial affection divorced from self-preservation does not amount to a Mr. LANCASTER.
very great deal. It is the boy, the young man, which makes the best use of his opportunity and the gifts with which he has been endowed, and who shows a disposition to carve out his own future and to paddle his own canoe who is always dearest to the mother's heart.
Yes, because she expects that if some burglar or horse thief waylays her, this young man, because he is her son, will come to her relief. This love is just commencing according to the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McLean). What kind of love is the boy to have for his mother? When it has arrived at its completion? Because he is twenty-one years of age does that mean that in spite of her love, and her up-bringing he is going to murder or assassinate her when his affection is complete? Is that the kind of love he is commencing to have for his mother?
The words used were not ' only commencing,' but were ' highly commendable.'
I am sorry if ' Hansard ' has done the hon. gentleman an injustice.
These words do not appear in the original, but in the corrected ' Hansard ' it is all right.

I am bound to accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but it is fair to ' Hansard,' that I should say that the words appearing there are:
It is quite proper that I should say that our love is only commencing.
I am not sure that the context would bear out the suggestion of the hon. gentleman. However, the hon. gentleman thought that there was some necessity of the boy, at some time, loving his mother, but that when he had become a big fellow, twenty-one years of age, thick in the chest, and doing well, and all this because of his mother's kindness, the mother's love and affection for her boy should only commence to bear fruition. To go a step further, we want to -see our boys and girls manifesting always an affection for their mothers and fathers, and the more there are of these the more strength we will have as a nation. You cannot disassociate the character of the nation from that of the individual. What the individuals are, so is the nation. It is absolutely impossible to be otherwise.
I wish to commend what the hon. member for Queens and Sunbury (Mr. H. H. McLean) said, although he has not said that he is going to flock alone. Although he has not taken a position very much different from that of the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmer3on), although he has not said that we should give aid in paroxysms and spasms, and although he has not said that this is necessary, he has

said that there is an emergency existing and that something should be done. I appeal to that hon. gentleman under these circumstances, before this vote is taken, and I ask him if he does not think that he, could carry out his views better by voting for the amendment of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. How can he, consistently with what he said, vote for this Bill? He has also said tha^ he believes-that this navy should be controlled by the mother country, and in that respect he is at daggers drawn with the government. Under those circumstances, I say that there can be no question in the mind of any intelligent, and fair minded member of this House, that the policy of the government is utterly impossible from a practical point of view. It is not practicable. If you are going to be in unison with the mother country, you cannot for five or ten years at least expect to give relief to any body. Hon. gentlemen opposite, in their emergency, as I say, and I think that they are in more of an emergency than Great Britain is, in one way, are considering how they can square their views with the necessity of voting for the government. We cannot help but laugh at the remarks of the right hon. leader of the government in introducing, and in moving the second reading of this Bill, in which he undertook to rail at the opposition, because they did not all express the same views upon this question. He forgot that the opposition, no matter what views they expressed, had not the ear of the Governor General, and could not bring in a Bill of this kind. He forgot that no matter what policy we proposed we could not, under the rules of the House, because we are not the advisers of His Excellency, introduce a Bill. But the right hon. gentleman has his own language coming back upon him because his supporters behind him are more at sea upon this question than we are, and there is more disunion among them than there is upon this side of the House. One hon. gentleman says that he would have to vote that the navy shall be controlled by Great Britain. That is my hon. friend from Queens and Sunbury (Mr. H. H. McLean). Another, the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), does not want a navy Bill at all, because he wants to give more grants to subsidize railways or dig a few canals. The hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Tur-eotte), says he ought to vote for this Bill, because it is going to bring independence. So we find that all these gentlemen are going to support the measure of the Prime Minister although they are not at one upon it. If the right hon. gentleman were well advised, if he were not determined to try and get in the thin edge of the wedge of independence for Canada by placing this Bill before the people, he would withdraw it.
As an imperialist, because I refuse to call him an anti-imperialist at the present time, although he says he is neither one nor the other, as a loyal citizen, and as the Prime Minister of Canada for the time being, I think he would be well advised if he withdrew this Bill, and go on with the domestic affairs of the country in parliament instead of interfering with the rights of Great Britain, as this measure must do. This measure must lead to independence, and for that reason, if for no other reason, my constituency would require me to vote against it. I am not talking about the Conservatives only of Lincoln and Niagara. Every intelligent Liberal as well as every intelligent Conservative in the constituency of Lincoln and Niagara would insist upon this being done if he really believed that it was going to lead to independence. When we find an hon. gentleman who is in the caucus of the right hon. Prime Minister, who knows what is going on, standing up here, and saying that that is the reason for his voting for this Bill, I think we are right in concluding that this measure is not one which this parliament should accept. An independent navy means an independent Canada. What else could it mean? The existence of Canada as a part of the British nation cannot be consistent with an independent navy. If you do not want an independent Canada, you do not want an independent navy because if you are to give Great Britain protection as it may be required you must put this navy under the control of the British authorities. We have heard a great deal about the pride and duty of Canada, and all that sort of thing, and there has been a great deal said about what we owe to Great Britain. In addition to what I have touched upon let us see what we owe to Great Britain. We owe everything we have here to Great Britain. Great Britain made us what we are. True we developed ourselves when we had the chance, true having got a start, we have gone ahead and expanded. Neither would the Prime Minister be sitting here nor would I be standing where I am if it were not for Great Britain. Great Britain made this country, Great Britain gave us our rights, her parliament passed the British North America Act, and said that we should do as we liked in respect to matters purely Canadian.
Great Britain's army and navy have protected us as they have protected our forefathers, and they have taught the world to know that if any hostile nation should interfere with Canada in her pursuit of the arts of peace, that nation would have to reckon with Great Britain. And what more has Great Britain done for us? For more than a century her navy has protected our commerce and enabled us to pursue in peace a policy which has tended so greatly to our

development. We have not paid a dollar for that army or for that navy of Great Britain, but that great strength has been behind us to warn pirates, confiseators and grabbers of territory to keep their hands off. What has Great Britain done for us? What would we amount to as a people today were it not that Great Britain has done for Canada that which she has done for every nation in which she has planted her flag? Great Britain has carried civilization and religion into every country, and proclaimed the doctrine that the weak are entitled to their rights as well as the strong. What would be our state of civilization in Canada to-day were it not that in past years we have lived under the British flag? I shall not now speak of sentiment; I shall put it on a lower plane. I shall speak from the material standpoint, and I will ask: How many of our wheat fields, how many of our factories would exist, how many of our people in all walks of life would have achieved their high stage of civilization under any other flag than the grand old Union Jack? Who protects the commerce of Canada, who guarantees that Canada shall pursue in peace her path of progress? Sir, oqr protection is to be found in the army and navy of Groat Britain, to which we have never contributed one cent as yet, but which, mark you, we might legally under our constitution be to-morrow compelled to contribute to. When a child is not manly enough to contribute to the support of his parent in need, that parent may, under process of law, compel him, and if Canada should persist in the mean policy of not contributing to the defence of the motherland (and her own defence as well), the day may come when we could be told by Great Britain: As you are not manly enough to do this of your own free will, we will impose a tax upon you and make you do it. And, Sir, if Great Britain did that, Great Britain would be acting strictly within her legal rights. But Great Britain has not done it in the past; she has trusted us to do our duty, and shall we fail? What has Great Britain done for Canada? Look around and you will find the answer. Get on board any railway train, go on board any boat, walk through our wheat fields, drive along any country lane, and you will see what Great Britain has done for Canada. Look at the manhood and the womanhood which exists in Canada to-day, and ask yourselves if we would have that civilization, that intelligence and that education in which we pride, under any other flag than the flag of England. The answers of every Canadian, irrespective of party, must be, no. Now, let me point out to hon. gentlemen that this is not the first time that a Prime Minister of Canada has undertaken to say that the British navy is entitled to some support from us. And, to show this, Mr. LANCASTER.
I shall quote an editorial in the Toronto ' Mail and Empire ' of December 4, 1909. I shall submit this article to hon. gentlemen opposite to show that when they talk about building a little navy that has got to run away as soon as the enemy approaches, and when they talk about doing something for Great Britain, Great Britain can very well say: [DOT]Why, you o^ve us a back debt which you have never paid, and the payment of which we have never pressed you for. Now, this article which I shall quote, because it expresses in better language than I could use, the point I wish to make, says:

That the idea of provision for naval defence is new some people believe. But the statutes of Canada tell a different story. By chapter 37 of the Consolidated Statutes of 1859 several thousand acre9 of land were vested in the ' commissioners for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland,' for ever in trust for the service of the said department. The lands so vested were described in the schedule to the Act as follows:-
1.	-288 acres in the county of Sherbrooke, county of Haldimand.
2.	-389 acres in the townships of Tiny and Tay, in the county of Simeoe.
3.	-8 acres and 2 roods at Point Erederiok, in the township of Pittsburgh, in the county of Frontenac.
4.	-4 acres on the west side of Meadow street, in the town plot of Gwillimbury, in the county of Simeoe.
5.	-3,000 acres at Point Pelee, in the township of Mersea, in the county of Essex.
6.	-200 acres in the township of Vespra, in the county of Simeoe.
7.	-500 acres on the Island of St. Joseph, Lake Huron.
8.	-106 acres on the said island in Lake Huron.
